rows.text:
The fundamental difference in performance bottlenecks between prompt processing and autoregressive decoding on a single consumer GPU stems from the distinct computational characteristics of each phase: prompt processing is compute-bound, while autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound.

During prompt processing (also known as the prefill phase), the model processes the entire input sequence in parallel. This involves performing large matrix multiplications where the batch size (sequence length) is high. Because the operations are dense and parallelizable, the GPU's Tensor Cores are fully utilized, making the throughput limited by the raw floating-point operations per second (FLOPS) of the hardware. In this phase, the GPU is working at peak computational capacity.

In contrast, autoregressive decoding generates tokens one at a time. For each new token, the model must load the entire set of model weights from GPU memory (VRAM) into the processing units to perform a single matrix-vector multiplication. Since the amount of computation per token is small relative to the size of the model, the GPU cores spend most of their time idle, waiting for data to be transferred from VRAM. Consequently, the speed of this phase is limited by the memory bandwidth of the GPU (measured in GB/s) rather than its computational power. Consumer GPUs
